title: Boston Children's Hospital reanalyzes unsolved rare-disease genomes with OpenAI's o3 Deep Research and confirms 18 diagnoses, 11 of them new
summary: OpenAI's o3 Deep Research helped Boston Children's Hospital reanalyze 376 locally unresolved rare-disease cases, which yielded 18 confirmed diagnoses: 11 new and seven rediscoveries.
account: Researchers at Boston Children’s Hospital and OpenAI used o3 Deep Research to reassess 376 rare-disease cases that remained unresolved in their local research records. NBC News reported that the team ran the 376 genomes through o3 in 2025. The paper names the model snapshot o3-deep-research-2025-05-28. Clinicians reviewed candidates, arranged laboratory confirmation, and returned results to families. Kyra Benton told NBC News that a researcher from the lab called her with news of her diagnosis in the summer of 2025. NBC News published its report on 18 June 2026. It interviewed Benton about receiving a diagnosis and sought comment from outside clinicians. In the paper, published on 25 June 2026, the researchers reported 18 confirmed local diagnoses, or 4.8%: 11 newly identified diagnoses and seven rediscoveries of diagnoses already made elsewhere. The authors explain in their discussion that some findings depended on later gene discoveries, revised classifications, previously uncalled variants, or information that was unavailable to earlier analyses. They did not compare the model with a simultaneous expert reanalysis using the same current evidence. They also did not measure improvements in treatment, cost, or clinician time. The study was retrospective and involved OpenAI employees and funding. It therefore does not establish an independent estimate of the model’s added benefit.
purpose: OpenAI o3 Deep Research is a general-purpose reasoning and research model. The Manton Center team built an explanation-first reanalysis workflow around it to propose candidate molecular diagnoses for unsolved cases. These diagnoses were the workflow's intended output. OpenAI states that the study does not describe or endorse a customer use of o3 for diagnosis. Brownstein said that she was shocked that a commercial system could find new diagnoses in genomes analyzed many times.
system: OpenAI o3 Deep Research, used as the reasoning layer of an LLM-assisted genome reanalysis workflow (Human Phenotype Ontology terms, clinician notes and a filtered variant table in; explanation-linked candidate diagnoses out)
deployer: Boston Children's Hospital, The Manton Center for Orphan Disease Research (with Harvard Medical School and OpenAI co-authors)
segment: Hospital rare-disease research center; retrospective reanalysis study

ratings.reason: Investigators returned 18 confirmed local diagnoses to families, including 11 new diagnoses and seven rediscoveries. In an interview with NBC News, a patient describes the value of receiving an explanation after years of uncertainty. Changes to treatment or health outcomes were not measured.

The team resolved 18 cases in its local research records, including seven diagnoses already established elsewhere. The study made no simultaneous comparison with a human reanalysis and measured no savings in time, cost or clinician effort.

ai_role.statement: o3 Deep Research read each de-identified case packet and proposed the most plausible molecular explanation with its supporting evidence. It diagnosed no one. Humans did the rest. At least two reviewers adjudicated each candidate under ACMG/AMP criteria, a CLIA-certified laboratory confirmed each variant, and the clinical team returned results to families. Its distinct contribution was surfacing candidates in cases that commercial and institutional analyses and multidisciplinary teams had already reviewed. In one early-psychosis case it inferred a 22q11.2 deletion absent from the input data, which genome sequencing then confirmed. Seven of the 18 were rediscoveries already established externally. The study was retrospective, and reviewers were not blinded to model confidence. The authors call for prospective evaluation with comparator baselines, so the gain over renewed human reanalysis is unmeasured.

fields.summary: OpenAI's o3 Deep Research helped Boston Children's Hospital reanalyze 376 locally unresolved rare-disease cases, which yielded 18 confirmed diagnoses: 11 new and seven rediscoveries.
fields.account: Researchers at Boston Children’s Hospital and OpenAI used o3 Deep Research to reassess 376 rare-disease cases that remained unresolved in their local research records. NBC News reported that the team ran the 376 genomes through o3 in 2025. The paper names the model snapshot o3-deep-research-2025-05-28. Clinicians reviewed candidates, arranged laboratory confirmation, and returned results to families. Kyra Benton told NBC News that a researcher from the lab called her with news of her diagnosis in the summer of 2025. NBC News published its report on 18 June 2026. It interviewed Benton about receiving a diagnosis and sought comment from outside clinicians. In the paper, published on 25 June 2026, the researchers reported 18 confirmed local diagnoses, or 4.8%: 11 newly identified diagnoses and seven rediscoveries of diagnoses already made elsewhere. The authors explain in their discussion that some findings depended on later gene discoveries, revised classifications, previously uncalled variants, or information that was unavailable to earlier analyses. They did not compare the model with a simultaneous expert reanalysis using the same current evidence. They also did not measure improvements in treatment, cost, or clinician time. The study was retrospective and involved OpenAI employees and funding. It therefore does not establish an independent estimate of the model’s added benefit.

produced_by: Already-sequenced unsolved cases, mostly child-parent trios, assembled into a de-identified packet. Each packet held Human Phenotype Ontology terms, any clinician notes, age and sex. It also held a filtered variant table with rarity, predicted effect, ClinVar class and family signal quality
A general-purpose reasoning model asked for the single most plausible molecular explanation and its evidence, not just a ranked gene. The prompt was refined first on cases of known diagnosis
Time elapsed since the original analysis, so that newly published gene-disease links and reclassified variants existed to be found
Expert adjudication under ACMG/AMP criteria by at least two reviewers, CLIA-laboratory confirmation, and return of results by the clinical team
must_hold: Human geneticists review every candidate and a model output is never treated as a diagnosis
Confirmatory testing in a certified laboratory before any result reaches a family
De-identified data handled inside approved environments
Yield expectations calibrated to the cohort: single-digit gains in heavily reviewed cases, and seven of the 18 here were rediscoveries
